title: The B2B SaaS Website Readiness Score
subtitle: Find out whether your website is winning you deals or quietly costing you them — and exactly where to focus next.

questions.text: If a prospect sees your website before a sales call, what typically happens?

answers.label: They cancel, don't show, or arrive very confused about what we do
They arrive but seem uncertain about what we actually offer
They show up with okay expectations but a few misalignments
They arrive pre-warmed and ask good, informed questions
They show up already sold on us and reference specific things they saw

questions.text: How well does your current brand reflect the stage your company is actually at today?

answers.label: We look like a side project; we've grown well past this
Still feels early-stage; we're further along than the brand suggests
Close, but it still feels like last year's version of us
Mostly landing; misses some of where our product has moved
Visitors immediately understand our ambition and take us seriously

questions.text: How often do prospects mistake you for a smaller or less credible company than you are?

answers.label: Nearly every intro call involves correcting this impression
More often than I'd like
Occasionally, and usually cleared up quickly
Rarely — when it happens it's not really about the brand
Almost never; our brand earns its room in the conversation

low.headline: Your website is selling yesterday's company
low.text: There is a gap between what your product actually is and what your site communicates — and prospects are feeling it before you have said a word. This is not about aesthetics. It is about the credibility cost of asking someone to take you seriously while your site tells a different story. Every intro call where you are correcting a misperception is a call your website should have handled.
steps: Audit your hero section against where your company actually is today — not where it was when you last redesigned
List the three most common misperceptions you hear on intro calls, then check whether your homepage is creating them
Submit your URL for a free hero redesign — we will show you what the gap looks like closed in five days, no strings attached

mid.headline: You are close, but the brand is lagging behind the product
mid.text: Your positioning is not wrong, but it is not current. The product has moved; the site has not kept pace. That gap shows up on calls where you spend time correcting perceptions that a sharper site would have handled before the calendar invite was accepted.
steps: Identify the two or three things that have changed most about your product in the last 12 months
Check your hero section: does it reflect those things, or does it still describe where you were?
Book a homepage audit — we will tell you exactly which pages are holding back your credibility and what to fix first

high.headline: Your brand is doing real work — keep it earning
high.text: Your brand is aligned with where your company is, and prospects feel that before the first call. The risk from here is sitting still. Brand-product fit degrades as the product moves forward and the site does not. Build a regular review cycle now, before the gap opens again.
steps: Set a quarterly hero section review against new product releases and recent client wins
Document the exact language your best clients use to describe you — that belongs on your site, not in a Notion doc
Identify where on-demand design support could help you keep the site current as the product evolves

questions.text: A first-time visitor lands on your homepage. Within 10 seconds, can they tell exactly who you are for and what you do?

answers.label: Probably not — we hear 'what exactly do you do?' on most first calls
Our category is clear but our specific buyer is not obvious
Most people get it, but we lose some visitors right at the hero
Clear for our core buyer; occasionally misses on edge cases
We regularly hear 'this is exactly what I was looking for'

questions.text: How specifically does your hero section speak to the pain your buyer is in right now?

answers.label: It mostly describes us — what we do, our values — not their problem
It mentions their category but not their actual situation
It names the problem but in language we share with every competitor
It names the problem and hints at our specific angle on it
It names their exact situation in words they would use themselves

questions.text: Compared to your three closest competitors, how differentiated does your website messaging look?

answers.label: We look similar — I could not name our differentiator from the copy alone
We have a different angle but it is buried below the fold
We stand out in one area but are fairly generic everywhere else
Our positioning is clear and defensible across most pages
Our site is the one prospects send their co-founder saying 'this is how we should position'

low.headline: Your messaging is describing you, not converting them
low.text: If your homepage talks more about what you do than about the problem your buyer is living with right now, you are losing them in the first 10 seconds. The most common version of this: a hero that lists capabilities without ever naming the specific pain. Visitors do not convert from competence claims. They convert when they feel seen.
steps: Rewrite your hero headline to name the specific situation your best clients were in before they found you
Pull exact phrases from your last five sales calls where clients described their problem — those belong in your copy
Submit your URL for a free hero redesign to see what sharper messaging looks like in your actual context

mid.headline: You are getting the category right but missing the buyer specifics
mid.text: People understand what you do, but not why you are the right choice for them specifically. The fix is usually moving from capability language to situation language — less 'we design websites for SaaS companies' and more 'you have outgrown your website and it is getting in the way of sales.'
steps: Write down the three most common client situations that led to hiring you — make those the lead in your hero section
Check whether your differentiator is visible above the fold or hidden in an about page nobody reads
Book a homepage audit to identify exactly which messaging gaps are costing you conversions

high.headline: Your messaging is doing the qualifying work for you
high.text: You are in the minority of B2B SaaS sites that speaks to a specific buyer in specific language. That earns you better qualified inbound and shorter sales cycles. The next move is making sure it stays current as your ICP sharpens and your product evolves.
steps: Review your hero copy every six months against your last 10 closed deals — does it still describe who is actually converting?
Look for pages below the hero (features, pricing, case studies) where messaging quality may have drifted
Consider whether your current positioning would hold up in a new segment you are moving into

questions.text: How does your website perform as a sales tool between conversations?

answers.label: It does not — people only engage after I have spoken to them directly
It occasionally confirms what I have said on a call
We get some inbound but most leads still need heavy qualification
It handles a meaningful portion of pre-qualification before the first call
Our site generates qualified inbound consistently without us doing anything

questions.text: How often do you proactively use your website in the sales process itself?

answers.label: Rarely — I would rather walk them through a deck
Sometimes, as a back-up reference after a call
We send it but do not rely on it to do much selling work
We direct prospects to specific pages that handle real objections
Our website is central to the sales process and we treat it that way

questions.text: How many unique visitors does your website get per month?
questions.hint: Check your analytics dashboard — Google Analytics, Plausible, or Fathom. A rough estimate is fine.

questions.text: What is your average client retainer or project value in £ per month?
questions.hint: For one-off projects, divide the total project value by 12 to get a monthly equivalent.

low.headline: Your website is a brochure, not a sales asset
low.text: If you are still sending decks because you do not trust your site to do the work, or if prospects only engage after a call, you are doing sales manually at every stage. Every qualified prospect who lands on your site before speaking to you is a test. Right now most of them are leaving without converting.
steps: List the three most common objections you handle on calls and check whether your website addresses any of them
Create at least one page or section that speaks directly to your best buyer's specific situation, not just your services
Submit your URL for a free hero redesign to see what it looks like when your site starts the sales conversation for you

mid.headline: Your site is in the conversation — now make it earn its keep
mid.text: You are sending prospects to your website and it is doing some work, but it is not yet handling the heavy lifting. The gap between 'confirms what I said on a call' and 'pre-qualifies before the call' is usually in the specificity of the messaging and the quality of the conversion path.
steps: Map the journey from homepage to booking a call — count the clicks, read the copy at each step, look for where you lose people
Add one page or section specifically designed to handle your single most common sales objection
Send your website URL to prospects before a call this week and ask them what questions it raised — those gaps are your content brief

high.headline: Your website is pulling its weight in the sales process
high.text: You are in the group where the website is genuinely contributing to sales outcomes, not just existing. The next lever is usually improving the quality of inbound rather than the volume — sharper targeting, cleaner qualification, and more specific case study content.
steps: Review your case studies: are they outcome-led with real numbers, or are they still describing the process?
Look at which pages have the highest exit rates — those are the ones losing qualified prospects who arrived ready
Consider an on-demand design support retainer to keep the site current as your sales positioning sharpens

answers.label: We have a 'Contact Us' button somewhere; that is about it
We have CTAs but they are all the same and have never been tested
We have thought about it but have not run any real tests
We have tested our primary CTA and have data on what works
We run continuous CTA tests across multiple pages with clear, tracked results

questions.text: How well do your CTAs match where a visitor actually is in their buying decision?

answers.label: We ask everyone for the same commitment regardless of where they are
We have 'get in touch' and 'learn more' but nothing more strategic than that
We try to differentiate hard vs soft CTAs but it is based on instinct not data
We use a mix of hard and soft CTAs mapped to different intent levels
Every CTA maps to a buyer stage and we have data on what each one is doing

questions.text: What percentage of website visitors currently submit a demo request, trial signup, or contact form?
questions.hint: Total monthly form submissions ÷ total monthly visitors × 100. A typical B2B SaaS homepage converts at 1–3%.

questions.text: How confident are you that your homepage is converting as well as it could be right now?

answers.label: Not at all — I know there is significant conversion being left on the table
Low confidence — I have not looked seriously at the data
Uncertain — we get conversions but I could not tell you if that is good or not
Fairly confident — we have done some work here and have rough benchmarks
Very confident — we track it closely and our numbers are strong

low.headline: Your CTAs are asking everyone for everything — and converting no one
low.text: A single 'Contact Us' button asks a cold visitor for the same commitment as someone who has been on three calls with you. The gap between hard CTAs (book a call, start a trial) and soft CTAs (free audit, see examples) is often the difference between a site that converts at 1% and one that converts at 4%. You are leaving qualified prospects on the table every day.
steps: Identify which of your current CTAs are hard (high commitment) and which are soft (low commitment) — and whether you have both
Add one low-friction soft CTA to your hero section for visitors who are not ready to book a call yet
Get a free homepage audit from us: we will tell you exactly which CTA changes would move your conversion rate

mid.headline: You have CTAs — now make them work harder with data
mid.text: You have thought about conversion, but without testing there is a ceiling on how far instinct takes you. The optimal button text, the right mix of hard and soft CTAs, the placement on the page — these are answerable with data. Right now you are leaving some of that on the table.
steps: Run a simple A/B test on your primary CTA text — even two weeks of data with basic analytics will tell you something useful
Map your pages to buyer intent: high-intent pages (pricing, case studies) get hard CTAs; discovery pages get soft
Book a homepage audit to get specific, data-grounded CTA recommendations for your site

high.headline: Your conversion thinking is ahead of most B2B SaaS sites
high.text: You are testing, mapping intent, and tracking results. That is not common. The next level is usually extending this discipline beyond the homepage to case study pages, feature pages, and content pages where buying intent can be high but the CTA is typically an afterthought.
steps: Audit your secondary pages (case studies, integrations, features) for CTA relevance and intent match
Check whether your soft CTAs are genuinely low-friction or whether they are still asking for more than the visitor is ready to give
Look at exit pages in your analytics — where are high-intent visitors leaving without converting?

answers.label: Months — or it never gets updated at all
Several weeks and significant back-and-forth with whoever manages the site
A couple of weeks if we make it a priority
About a week with some friction in the process
Days — our setup makes it straightforward to ship updates fast

questions.text: How easily can your team update copy and design on the website without going to a developer?

answers.label: Nothing gets changed without a developer; it is a bottleneck we have accepted
Technically possible but painful enough that we avoid it
Basic copy changes are fine; anything visual requires outside help
The team handles most updates and escalates only the bigger changes
Fully self-sufficient — we move fast without needing external resource

low.headline: Your website cannot keep up with your company — and that gap is compounding
low.text: When it takes months to update your site after a major win or product launch, prospects are seeing an outdated version of your company every single day. The harder your product team works, the wider the gap gets. This is not a design problem — it is a process and infrastructure problem. The answer is a website setup that moves as fast as your business does.
steps: Identify the last three significant wins or product updates that are not reflected on your site and add them this week
Work out whether your current CMS or platform is the constraint, or whether it is a process and resource gap
Ask us about Webflow development and migration — it is specifically built for teams that need to move without a developer in the loop

mid.headline: You can update the site — but it costs you time you do not have
mid.text: The ability to update is there, but the friction means you are making trade-off calls: is this update worth the two-week turnaround? That calculus is slowly letting your site fall behind. The real cost is not the update you cannot make — it is the one you decide is not worth the hassle.
steps: Map the actual process for making a change to your site — count the steps, the people, and the days
Identify the one type of update you avoid most because of friction — that is your first priority to fix
Look at on-demand design support as a way to remove the bottleneck without the overhead of a full-time hire

high.headline: You have the velocity — use it as a competitive advantage
high.text: Moving fast on your website is a genuine edge that most B2B SaaS companies do not have. The companies that stay ahead are the ones that ship new case studies quickly, update their messaging when the ICP shifts, and reflect new product capabilities before competitors notice. You have the infrastructure. Keep using it deliberately.
steps: Make a quarterly website update a standing agenda item — planned, not reactive
Build a running library of updated product shots, client quotes, and feature highlights so updates take minutes, not days
Consider a CRO optimisation retainer to keep the conversion layer improving at the same pace as the design

cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
